analysis.one_liner: Requires warning labels on children's toys with small parts stating which ages face danger.
analysis.headline: The Toy Safety and Child Protection Act died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Consumer Product Safety Commission to require warning labels on toys containing small parts. The label would have to state which ages of children the toy is not intended for and describe the specific danger — such as choking — for children in that age range. The Commission would have had to set the standard by January 1, 1990, and could use its existing enforcement powers against toys sold without the label.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and caregivers of young children, especially toddlers, who would get clear on-package warnings about small parts that can choke or otherwise harm children too young for the toy. Pediatricians and child-safety advocates also gain a standardized disclosure tool.

how_it_helps.text: The Consumer Product Safety Commission must issue a standard requiring that packaging and accompanying materials of any toy containing small parts carry a cautionary label stating the ages for which the toy is not intended and describing the dangerous property and its hazardous consequences [S3].

Labels must be prominently displayed, visible and noticeable, in English, and include the word 'WARNING' in capital letters, and the Commission may enforce the standard with any remedy available under the Federal Hazardous Substances Act [S3].

The bill amends the Federal Hazardous Substances Act so that a toy containing small parts that is not properly labeled is itself treated as a hazardous substance, giving the Commission leverage over unlabeled toys [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Toy manufacturers and importers bear the cost of designing and printing compliant warning labels on packaging and descriptive materials, a cost that can be passed partly to consumers through slightly higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes labeling and compliance costs on toy manufacturers and importers, which are partly passed on to consumers in prices [S3].
The required labels must be in English, so the warning may not reach caregivers who do not read English [S3].
Labels warn about hazards but do not remove them: a toy with a choking hazard stays on the market, and the protection depends on the adult reading and heeding the packaging.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A modest, low-cost disclosure rule aimed at one of the most serious toy hazards — small parts that can choke toddlers — with the main drawbacks being modest labeling costs for manufacturers and an English-only label requirement that limits its reach. The design is simple and would likely have been inexpensive relative to the safety information gained, though it protects through warnings rather than by removing hazards.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 101st Congress ended without a hearing, a vote, or even one cosponsor.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Dodd introduced the Toy Safety and Child Protection Act in the Senate on February 9, 1989 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day, and the record shows no further action [S5].
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill was never reported out of committee or brought to a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Toy manufacturers and importers avoided a new federal labeling mandate, while parents gained nothing because the warning-label requirement never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Toy makers who avoided new labeling rules

for.name: Sen. Christopher J. Dodd
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Toy Safety and Child Protection Act in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it was never reported out of committee or scheduled for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill attracted no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is unknown from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have required redesigned warning labels on packaging and descriptive materials for any toy containing small parts, a compliance cost. The industry's interest in avoiding the mandate ran against the safety information parents would have gained.
Retailers would have had to ensure stocked toys carried compliant labels, but clear age warnings could reduce returns, injuries, and liability from toys given to the wrong age child.
